messages.author: 52c5febb78eca8a4
messages.subject: boundary constraint
parts:
I'm estimating a model with INLA using SPDEs and I would compare my results respect a GAM's with a "soap film smoother" for the spatial effect. With SOAP it's possible to insert a constraint on the boundary. Can I do the same thing with INLA? In particular, I would predictions and spatial effect equal to zero on the boundary and beyond the reference domain. It's possible?
Thanks!

messages.author: 9a89594e7fcb7aad
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] boundary constraint
parts:
On Sun, 2015-05-03 at 15:48 +0100, Daniel Simpson wrote:
> A cheap hack would be to set a new likelihood with fixed high
> precision that observes a zero at each of the boundary nodes and use
> the INLA syntax for multiple livelihoods.

Just a minor comment to this issue.

If you want to define some of the nodes in a modelcomponent to some
fixed values, an easier trick (which will give the correct normalization
constant), is to define this as

Ax = e

and define this in 'extraconstr'. This will add one 'solve' for each
constr. However, since defining x[1] = 1, f.ex, will make that model
component singular, you need to add some noise, like

f(..., diagonal = 1e-8)

which will ensure that x[1] = 1, say, almost (like observed with a high
variance).

ensuring that x[1] = 1, say, using an additional likelihood, would be a
little more cumbersome, will not adjust the normalising constant of that
model component, BUT, but be computationally cheaper.

H

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] boundary constraint
parts:
> On 3 May 2015, at 17:24, Håvard Rue <hr...@r-inla.org> wrote:
>
>> On Sun, 2015-05-03 at 15:48 +0100, Daniel Simpson wrote:
>> A cheap hack would be to set a new likelihood with fixed high
>> precision that observes a zero at each of the boundary nodes and use
>> the INLA syntax for multiple livelihoods.

If this is done one the mesh boundary itself, you will get both values _and_ normal derivatives equal to zero on the boundary, which is probably not the desired effect. However, if the mesh has an extension beyond the desired zero-boundary, then it should give a reasonable approximation of Dirichlet, if you then just ignore everything outside of the zero-curve.

> If you want to define some of the nodes in a modelcomponent to some
> fixed values, an easier trick (which will give the correct normalization
> constant), is to define this as
>
> Ax = e

There will be quite a few of these (order sqrt(n)), so this is likely to be more expensive than the dual likelihood approach.

However, back to the original question: no, the proper way of doing this still doesn't have a direct interface. It needs a bit of programming of the same kind used for 1D models, where the user can choose between Neumann, dirichlet, free, and cyclic boundaries. It's not a technically difficult thing, but many small parts of the code will be affected so I need some focused time to do it.

If you only need a simple spline-like model ( kappa=0 ) it's easier, and directly calling the inla.spde2.generic function is an option.
One would then first construct the precision matrix for the free boundary problem (I'll need to get back to you on the needed inla.fmesher.smorg() call to do that), and remove the rows& columns corresponding to the boundary nodes and use as input to a "generic0" model, and construct A matrices for the full mesh and then remove the corresponding columns. The summary.random output will contain only the interior nodes.

Finn

Thanks to all for your input on this! 
The problem of boundaries came-up when estimating the excursion sets which are dependent on the size of the total area. We needed to predict a process in the sea, but our original mesh included locations on land (to deal with the boundary effect). The model estimated large values on land and consequently, resulted in smaller size sets over the area we were interested in i.e., the sea. So now, I modified the mesh using the coastline - hard boundary. In this case, having a process equal to 0 at the coastline would be ideal. Right now, some of my models are predicting some ‘crazy' values in locations near the coastlines (new boundary). 
So, if applicable, I’m happy to test the inla.spde2.generic function. Finn, if you have some codes that I could look through, I would be interested!
Thank you
A

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] boundary constraint
parts:
Hi,

I've attached code for running Dirichlet boundary models.
The syntax for the helper functions is basically the same as for the
regular functions,
but it supports just a small subset of the features.
The code runs both Neumann and Dirichlet models, so you can see the differences.

I believe the latest excursions package contains features helping with
extracting the relevant
parts of the predictor, this works in exactly the same way for Neumann
and Dirichlet
models, since the predictions are not tied to the internal size of the
model itself.
It's only when looking at summary.random$field that the user will
notice any difference.

The example also compares what happens for simple model
misspecification; running a
Neumann model on Dirichlet data, and a Dirichlet model on Neumann data.
At least for the simple boundary in the example, it's safer to use a Neumann
model, but it may be different for more complicated models.

Note that the example includes an intercept, so that the complete model can have
an arbitrary value on the boundary. For true Neumann, just don't
include the intercept.

The example does not support soap film smoothing, since that would
involve a model
for the boundary values as well. This is also doable, but messier, as
it will involve more
parameters. Future inla version may include that.

Finn

> Thanks to all for your input on this!
> The problem of boundaries came-up when estimating the excursion sets which
> are dependent on the size of the total area. We needed to predict a process
> in the sea, but our original mesh included locations on land (to deal with
> the boundary effect). The model estimated large values on land and
> consequently, resulted in smaller size sets over the area we were interested
> in i.e., the sea. So now, I modified the mesh using the coastline - hard
> boundary. In this case, having a process equal to 0 at the coastline would
> be ideal. Right now, some of my models are predicting some ‘crazy' values in
> locations near the coastlines (new boundary).
>
>
> But dirichlet boundaries would not allow a large values close to the
> coastline, which may or may not be realistic. Neumann boundaries should
> still be sensible; if your coastline is very irregular however, the increase
> in variance may be problematic, and that is perhaps what you're seeing.
> Having a mesh that extends inland should not be a problem, you just need to
> exclude those regions from the further analysis, by forcibly setting them to
> zero, and with zero variance, in the inla output.
> If you're using the excursions package to calculate the excursion sets,
> there is also an option to specify only a subset of the model to operate on.
>

>

> Finn

> call to do that), and remove the rows& columns corresponding to the boundary
> nodes and use as input to a "generic0" model, and construct A matrices for
> the full mesh and then remove the corresponding columns. The summary.random
> output will contain only the interior nodes.
>
>
>
> On May 4, 2015, at 7:15 AM, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
> On 3 May 2015, at 17:24, Håvard Rue <hr...@r-inla.org> wrote:
>
> On Sun, 2015-05-03 at 15:48 +0100, Daniel Simpson wrote:
> A cheap hack would be to set a new likelihood with fixed high
> precision that observes a zero at each of the boundary nodes and use
> the INLA syntax for multiple livelihoods.
>
>
> If this is done one the mesh boundary itself, you will get both values _and_
> normal derivatives equal to zero on the boundary, which is probably not the
> desired effect. However, if the mesh has an extension beyond the desired
> zero-boundary, then it should give a reasonable approximation of Dirichlet,
> if you then just ignore everything outside of the zero-curve.
>
> If you want to define some of the nodes in a modelcomponent to some
> fixed values, an easier trick (which will give the correct normalization
> constant), is to define this as
>
> Ax = e
>
>
> There will be quite a few of these (order sqrt(n)), so this is likely to be
> more expensive than the dual likelihood approach.
>
> However, back to the original question: no, the proper way of doing this
> still doesn't have a direct interface. It needs a bit of programming of the
> same kind used for 1D models, where the user can choose between Neumann,
> dirichlet, free, and cyclic boundaries. It's not a technically difficult
> thing, but many small parts of the code will be affected so I need some
> focused time to do it.
>
> If you only need a simple spline-like model ( kappa=0 ) it's easier, and

> Finn

> f(..., diagonal = 1e-8)
>
> which will ensure that x[1] = 1, say, almost (like observed with a high

> and Dirichlet
> models, since the predictions are not tied to the internal size of the
> model itself.
> It's only when looking at summary.random$field that the user will
> notice any difference.
>
> The example also compares what happens for simple model
> misspecification; running a
> Neumann model on Dirichlet data, and a Dirichlet model on Neumann data.
> At least for the simple boundary in the example, it's safer to use a Neumann
> model, but it may be different for more complicated models.
>
> Note that the example includes an intercept, so that the complete model can have
> an arbitrary value on the boundary. For true Neumann, just don't
> include the intercept.
>
> The example does not support soap film smoothing, since that would
> involve a model
> for the boundary values as well. This is also doable, but messier, as
> it will involve more
> parameters. Future inla version may include that.

> Finn
